patches.old: A surgeon increases the bending angle of the fiber beyond the critical angle from the inside of the core.
patches.new: A surgeon bends the fiber so sharply that some rays now meet the core–cladding interface at angles smaller than the critical angle.
patches.reason: As written the stem contradicted its own keyed answer. Striking the interface *beyond* the critical angle is the condition that preserves total internal reflection; what makes light escape — and what the keyed answer and its explanation describe — is rays arriving at angles *below* the critical angle once the fiber is bent sharply. A student reasoning correctly from the stem would conclude that nothing is lost.

patches.old: The image is **laterally inverted** (left–right reversed) but not inverted top-to-bottom.
patches.new: The image is **laterally inverted** (your raised left hand appears as the image's right) but not inverted top-to-bottom. Strictly, a plane mirror reverses neither left–right nor up–down but the axis running *into* the mirror — front becomes back. We read that depth flip as a left–right swap because we imagine ourselves turned around to face our image.
patches.reason: 'Laterally inverted' is the standard phrase and is kept, but on its own it invites the common misconception that a mirror treats the horizontal axis differently from the vertical one. Naming the actual front-to-back reversal answers the conceptual version of this question, which is the form the MCAT uses, without changing the terminology a student will meet elsewhere.

visual.title: Snell's law, the two-ray construction, and where the focus lands
visual.alt: A ray crossing from air into water and bending toward the normal, with Snell's law and the critical-angle condition and values for glass, water and diamond; a converging lens with a parallel ray refracted through the far focus and a ray straight through the centre, meeting at a real inverted image, with the thin lens equation; a table of sign conventions for lenses and mirrors; and two eyes, one too long with the focus falling short of the retina and one too short with the focus behind it.
visual.caption: Everything follows from one rule and one convention: light bends toward the normal entering a slower medium, and angles are measured from the normal rather than the surface. Two rays — one parallel, one through the centre — are enough to place any image.
